utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. I will have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Turone and Ms. Van Dusschoten for the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: For the defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. With me in the team is my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic, defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. My co-counsel is my colleague, Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, I am defending Mr. Hazim Delic. With me is Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman and along with my co-counsel Cynthia McMurray, we appear on behalf of the defendant Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Residovic , I think you were still continuing your cross-examination. Kindly remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, may I remind you you are still under oath. HRISTO VUKALO (continued)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Vukalo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you had a rest after yesterday, which must have been a tiring day for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have rested and it was not tiring.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We will resume where we stopped yesterday. We were discussing the defence in your village and your participation in that defence, and the statements that you made before coming here to testify in the district court in Belgrade and to the investigator of the prosecution from The Hague. For us to be able to have an easier time, and to make it clear to you that I do not have any intention of confusing you, I would like to refresh your memory with a copy of this statement that you made in Belgrade, and the statement that you made to the investigator of the International Tribunal, so that when I ask you something about these statements, you can yourself find the place that I am referring to, so I would like to ask the usher for his assistance to give the witness copies of these statements. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statements have been marked D60/1 A, B and C.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, will you look at the statement written in Cyrillic script. It says "Minutes on the Hearing of a Witness"; do you see your signature on every page of this statement in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that is the statement that you made to the investigating judge of the district court in Belgrade that we were referring to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but whether everything is quite correct I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at this statement in English now, another statement? Is that the statement that you signed each page of in Latin script?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that is the statement you made to the investigator of the OTP; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably; it must be.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that statement, you also have a translation into the Serbian language of the same statement. The date is 13th November 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To be even more precise about this statement, will you please turn to the last page of the Serbian text, where it says "Witness Acknowledgment"? That same certificate is to be found on the last page of the English text, where your signature is, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does it say there that: "This statement has been read over to me in the Serbian language and is true to the best of my recollection. I have given this statement voluntarily and I am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law committed in the territory of the Former Yugoslavia since 1991, and that I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now continue with the questions where we left off yesterday. Will you please turn to page 2 of the statement you made to the investigating judge in Belgrade and to see whether in paragraph 2 of that statement it says: "In order to protect ourselves and our lives, the lives of the members of our families and our property, we organised ourselves for defence with the little weapons we had. We kept guard duty so as not to be attacked by surprise." I have just read a part of the text to be found there. Will you tell me please: yesterday you stated in court that the inhabitants of your village did not organise defence, that you did not have any guard duty. Are these two different statements, Mr. Vukalo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said yesterday was that we did not have any weapons and we did not have any in the hamlet I was living in. As for this statement that I made, madam, when you recall something very unpleasant, I know I was crying, I had a very hard time. It was the first time I was being questioned after I had left the camp, so it was formulated more by the others. I was speaking in a disconnected manner, so this is not word by word what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, I will try to put to you very simple questions. Will you please look at the first page of the statement that you made to the investigator of the Hague Tribunal, the first one after the cover page, third paragraph, third sentence: "I believe there were some weapons in Donje Selo, but very little in my village. In Bjelovcina there were not more than 20 people under arms. Very little was done in preparation for defence because we had hoped that the JNA would protect us." Yesterday in court you said that there was no defence in the village of Bjelovcina, so my question is very simple. Will you please answer it for me? Is there a difference between what is said here in the statement that you made to the investigator of the Tribunal from what you stated here in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding the hamlet that I was living in, there was no defence, and it is impossible for the village to have had any proper defence because it is surrounded by seven, eight Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is very simple: can you see that what is contained in this statement made to the investigator of the International Tribunal in Belgrade and what you said here in the court are two different things? Is it different or not, that is the very simple question I am putting to you. Does what you said before differ from what you said here in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was some hunting weapons in the village of Bjelovcina. Anyway, I do not know. If there was any, I have no idea how much there was. I know that there were not many able-bodied men in the village of Bjelovcina, because the younger men were leaving. It was a village that had no asphalt road, people went away to work --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, but let me remind you: in answer to a question from the prosecution here in court as to whether there was any kind of organised defence at the time, you answered as follows: "I cannot talk about the organisation of defence. There were only 50 or 60 able-bodied men there." Then my colleague continued with the following question: "Did you participate in the defence of the village? Answer: On the part of the inhabitants of the village of Bjelovcina, I never heard then or later that they had put up any kind of resistance." So my question is: what you said as I have read out and what is written in the previous statement, do the two differ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no resistance from the village of Bjelovcina, no resistance. Some hunting weapons and personal pistols in private property, when I came to Celebici camp, I heard that these rifles had been given up, but I know there was no resistance and I do not see that it is possible to put up resistance, though I have really no idea about military strategy at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, will you please answer my question. Does what you said before and what you said in court differ?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This could go on all day. Counsel keeps asking the question, the witness gives an answer, counsel does not like the answer, it is not the answer she wants, so we go on and on and on again. The witness has given an answer. If that is not satisfactory to counsel, that is unfortunate; that is what often happens. This just amounts to harassment if it continues on forever, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, she has asked the question "does it differ", and that is pretty much a yes or no response. Either it differs or it does not. She has asked the question several times and has yet to receive one answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not understand why Mr. Moran is objecting. It is not his cross-examination. What is the basis of Mr. Moran's objection, standing up at this moment? I am sure that counsel can handle the situation herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms Residovic, I think you know what questions you have asked and what answers have been received to those questions. There is a way of going to the same question in a different way. The more you ask the same questions, you are likely to get the same answers, but you can find another way of getting a different answer if you want that. There is no way you can compel the person to give answers the way you want it, so perhaps you frame it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I thought that my question was a simple one that could be answered with a yes or a no, and that the witness would answer that question. I shall try in line with your advice to put the question again to the witness. Mr. Vukalo, the text I have read from the statement made to the prosecution truthfully reflects the statement you made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did I read it correctly is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You read what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have I correctly cited what you were asked by my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, as well as your answer to that question? Have I cited that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, I am answering to the best of my knowledge as to what I said in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question: did I correctly read out the question and the answer made here in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The two differ, do they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said "as far as i know". I cannot say something I do not know, but please let me, madam, finish my sentence. I am saying that this questioning was the first one since my release. I was crying, I was upset, and it is something extremely unpleasant and painful, so I do not know myself what I said, nor how it was formulated when it was written down. I suffered a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vukalo, would you please look again at the statement. Just a moment please -- the statement you made for the judge in Belgrade on page 2, paragraph 3, the second sentence. I am going to read it for you, so will you confirm that that is what it says there: "We put up resistance and the fighting lasted about one hour, but as they were superior, they broke up our defences so that we separated into groups and moved around in the surrounding woods until they captured us in the next day or two, together with the women and children." Is that what it says in this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says in this statement, but what it says here is not what I said. It is not what I said at all. How could there be any resistance when no one was hurt or killed on the side of the Muslim and Croat army that were attacking us? I learned that much later in the Celebici camp, that not one of the attackers was killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that when my colleague the Prosecutor asked you yesterday as follows: "Did you see or know anyone who was defending the village from the people who were attacking you?" Was your answer, Mr. Vukalo: "I did not hear a single shot coming from the village"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true; I did not hear a single shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then my colleague continued: "Was anyone engaged in the defence of the village? Answer: As concerns the inhabitants of the village of Bjelovcina, I did not hear that any kind of resistance was put up." Is that what you said in court here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there is a difference between the sentence that I read out to you a moment ago and what you said here in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said before this honourable court is what I said, I myself, and what is written here are not my words. That is maybe how it was understood and how it was formulated, but it is not what I said. This sentence that you read, there was no resistance, what kind of resistance? We were fleeing with the children, the women, the elderly; and the people who had hunting rifles, I heard later in the camp, they had surrendered them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Vukalo, a defence that lasted one hour and no defence at all are two different things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no defence in my hamlet for sure, and as I heard later on, there was no defence in the village as a whole. Nobody fired any weapons, and I certainly did not hear a single shot. That is as much as I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, can you please turn to page 3 of your statement for the investigating judge in Belgrade? I will read out from the third paragraph sentences to be found somewhere in the middle of that paragraph, so will you please try and find them: "After some time, Amir Dzelilovic came there, bringing with him Vlado Vukalo, who was carrying several rifles, and those were our rifles which we had left behind, and then they forced Vlado to go and collect them and he brought them over." Have I cited correctly the text to be found in that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have read it as it is written.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, will you please now look at the end of page 1 of the statement that you made for the investigator of the Hague Tribunal, the translation into Serbian? The last sentence on that first page reads, going over to the next page, as follows. I will read it out so please confirm it for me: "I decided to try and surrender to the friends of my relative Vlado from Kralupi, Dzelilovic Amir, because the soldiers were shooting at random. Vlado went to look for him. About 100 metres from Kralupi, we surrendered to Amir, and we gave up two rifles which we had kept to protect ourselves. All in all, there were 20 of us who surrendered, including my mother, an old woman who could hardly walk, and some infants." Is that the text to be found in the statement you made to the investigator of the prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What you read is written here, but I saw Vlado in Bozo Tomic's cellar, as I said yesterday. I do not know where he was going. That I do not know, but when I was taken there from Amir Dzelilovic's house, as I said yesterday, they took me there and in front of Gulas's house I was beaten up, and then they took me to Bozo Tomic's house, and I saw Vlado in the cellar of that house for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What I have read is to be found in the statement that you made to the investigator of the prosecution of the International Tribunal, MacLeod, Alistair, on 13th November 1996; is that correct? Yesterday, in answer to a question from my learned colleague the Prosecutor, you said -- the question was as follows: "When you went into the woods, did you take any weapons with you?" You answered: no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not take any weapons because I did not have any.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to the next question of my learned colleague, whether at the time of the attack you had any weapons in your house, you answered: "No, I did not." Is what you said to the Tribunal in Belgrade and to the investigator of the Hague Tribunal and what you have said to the Trial Chamber yesterday -- are they different statements? Do they look different? You have given your explanation. I am asking simply: is this different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was making the statement to the Hague Tribunal representative in Belgrade, I interrupted my statement on several occasions and Mr. MacLeod can remember that and he can confirm that, because I was crying. I was sobbing and I do not know how I was speaking, but what I said here yesterday was exactly the way it was, and I cannot say things I do not know, nor would I like to say anything I do not know. I can only tell you what I do know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, you are now saying that, because you were interrupted, because you were excited and distressed, that Mr. Alistair MacLeod was writing things which you did not actually say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was also an interpreter here. How could he understand everything? I do not know how he understood me, how he translated as I was sobbing, but what it says in the paper I do not agree with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, do you remember that yesterday, asked by my learned colleague the Prosecutor, when he asked you whether you were engaged or involved in any kind of military activity at the time prior to the military activities in 1992, at the very beginning of 1992, you answered "no".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I answered no, which is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at your statement to the investigating judge of the district court in Belgrade, page 2, where it says as follows, in the middle of the first sentence, and I only read that part of the sentence: "We organised ourselves for defence with some few weapons that we had. We had vigilante groups and guarded objects not to be attacked suddenly and unexpectedly."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what it says, but in my hamlet, there was no organised defence. Whether there were vigilante groups that was in the village, that was a kilometre from my hamlet, five more hamlets from our house and I do not know what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you, Mr. Vukalo, to look at the first page of your statement to the investigator of the International Tribunal. Look at the third paragraph . It begins like this: "A couple of days before the fighting began in the village, I received a rifle to defend my home. I received this from Dusko Bendzo, but I do not know where he received this from. I believe there were some weapons in Donje Selo and in my village very few. In Bjelovcina, there were not more than 20 armed people." Is that what your statement says, Mr. Vukalo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what the statement says on paper, yes. You read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, when asked by my learned colleague the Prosecutor -- did you not say clearly to this Tribunal that you had no rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I did not have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That you did not take it with you to the woods, that you did not have it in your home --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I did not. How could I have had it? How could I have taken it with me if I did not have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These answers that you gave to the Tribunal yesterday, are they not different from the words that I read from the statement that you gave to the investigator of the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, I learned when I was in the camp, Celebici camp -- I learned that people who had their hunting guns or pistols and so on, whatever people had, some people may have bought the weapons, but these weapons were in the village, but in my hamlet, I never saw a single gun, a single rifle. These were weapons that five people were the collective owners of a single rifle, but in my hamlet, we did not have anything and I cannot tell you anything. What I am saying now I only heard in the Celebici camp when I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukalo. We will not need the statements any more. I will ask you something else directly. Did you, Mr. Vukalo, have a heavy machine-gun of army issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the SDS party, in early April 1992, were you not informed by your acquaintances Miro Djurdjic and Spaso Babic that the SDS party had a task for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you yesterday how I became a member. Be patient with me and I will repeat that. I became a member because an elderly man from my village with many children, Djorde Bendzo -- he is 50 years old or more, alcoholic -- he went to the SDS offices, headquarters in the town, and he brought with him a heap of membership cards. He took some money for that and he spent it on alcohol. Actually, I was not a member of the SDS, only formally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, we heard your explanation that you gave to this tribunal, how you became a member, and everything you said is in the transcript and in the protocol, but now, to facilitate matters for us and for the court, please answer my question. Were you informed by Miro Djurdjic and Spaso Babic in early April 1992 that the SDS party has a task for you, an assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you after that, Mr. Vukalo, together with Dusko Bendzo, Dragan Sinic and Spaso Babic -- did you go with two cars, Skoda and Lada -- did you go to Dzelusa from where you took a Yugoslav army lorry and you brought the lorry full of weapons, rifles, M48, and two heavy machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never been to the village that you mentioned. I went to Konjic, I went to Sarajevo before the war, but to these villages down by the Neretva that you mentioned now, I never went. I have never been in that village in my life nor have I heard the name of that village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Vukalo, that after that, together with Dusko Bendzo and Dusan Tomic, you went to Borci and from the Yugoslav People's Army took over three heavy machine guns and two automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, at the moment when you were arrested, you said you also recognised some neighbours in HVO uniforms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the house of Jozic, called Aga, there was a command post for some of these units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were quite a number of soldiers there and from there they called for vans to come and collect us. I understood this was some kind of command post, I do not know what level. There were quite a number of soldiers who entered, who left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After spending the night in the motel, you were then taken to the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Celebici, according to your statements so far, you actually found some 7 to 12 young men from Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually found there are some 7, I do not know the exact number, but there were not more than ten people from Brdjani and from my village. I can repeat if necessary. I can repeat Scepo Vukalo, Veljko Babic, Ranko Dordic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The people from Brjdani told you they had been there for some 10 to 15 days already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, roughly. I do not remember exactly, but that is what they said, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vukalo, if on the 23rd you arrived in Celebici, would you then agree with me if I then say that these people must have been brought into the camp between 5th and 10th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, I arrived in Celebici on the 22nd, some time in the afternoon; I do not remember the exact hour. When they were brought to Celebici, I cannot tell you, but I know that they said, "We have been here for some 10 to 15 days", but we did not speak much about that. We were too frightened and we did not spend much time talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vukalo, I am just doing the mathematics. Anybody can do the mathematics. If you arrive on the 22nd, 10 to 15 days earlier would be between 5th and 10th May. That would roughly be the dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not do any mathematics; I only knew what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, you are a witness who is saying that they were imprisoned there and that they had been in prison from the day they were brought there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether they were there in the same place all the time. I found them there when I arrived and they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said, Mr. Vukalo, and I would like to just clarify this matter for myself -- you said that at first you were guarded by the military police of the HVO with white belts, and that included both Muslims and Croats; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it was the HVO, but the guards who were there when I arrived to room 22, they did wear white belts. Then I learned from other inmates -- Davor Bendzo knew Dzajic and he knew he was a Muslim. I also knew Mirsad Subasic, who actually was the first one to interrogate me and I knew he was a Muslim, but for the rest, they might have been Croats, they might have been Muslims; I do not know what they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the statement that you made in Celebici was the statement you made to Mirsad Subasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I made two or three statements to Mr. Subasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was at the very beginning of your arrival, soon after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mirsad Subasic was a member of the interior MUP of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know he actually completed studies of national defence or whatever. What he did and whether he worked for the police or in MUP I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that Miroslav Stenek was another of the men who -- he investigated you, plus another Croat who you think was the judge, presiding judge in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stenek interrogated us, the Croat whose name I cannot remember now. I used to know it but I cannot remember it now. I heard from the other inmates that he was something in the court in Konjic, the presiding judge or he did something in the court of law in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I might try to remind you: is that the man -- is that perhaps Goran Lokas, the man who was the presiding judge of the court in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Lokas, exactly. That is the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said these interrogators were actually treating you very fairly without abuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was first interrogated by Miro Stenek and by Lokas. During the interrogation, their conduct was fair, they did not hit us. Everybody else was hitting us but they were not hitting us. I would say they were fair and correct and as soon as they were not beating, I was satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, you also said that at one point, Mr. Subasic left that commission and that Miro Stenek and some other people continued to work as a commission for about a month to come, investigating you and the other inmates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first to investigate was Subasic from Idbar. After that, he disappeared, he was not there, he did not investigate us any more. Then came Mr. Miro Stenek after a while and the other person you mentioned, the Croat who was the presiding judge, Lokas; they continued the interrogation. For how long I do not know, but I would say that it did last for about 15 days up to a month, but I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I might suggest that this was until the end of June perhaps, because until the end of June or early July the commission was investigating and interrogating the inmates; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible, but I cannot confirm it with any degree of certainty, but it is very possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you said to the interrogators was written down in a statement, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but let me first say that I was hit, I was beaten, that I was totally scared, and I was beaten and beaten more, and this arm that had been injured in the motel and up there in the house of Bozo Tomic, it hurt horribly. I was terrified. I was practically beside myself, I did not have my wits about me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you signed that statement which you made before the investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had to sign it, I normally had to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a slight digression, Mr. Vukalo. We noticed when we inspected your statement in Belgrade that you signed it in the Cyrillic script; is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I am concerned, madam, the Cyrillic script and the Latin script which I both learned at school are both the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I know that, but you signed that statement in the Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The statement before the investigator of the International Tribunal you signed in the Latin script?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in fact now I see that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, my question is: to us in Bosnia-Herzegovina it was totally the same whether we wrote in Latin or Cyrillic script; is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I learned both scripts, the Cyrillic and the Latin and I could use both.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. So it is correct that for all of us, the inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina, both scripts were equal and we all knew them and we used them; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, I believe that all of these -- both scripts were taught in the whole of Yugoslavia; whether that is true you can also say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, very well, but we are now speaking -- referring to this nearer area where we lived. Very well, thank you. Mr. Vukalo, you said that somewhere towards the end of 1992, you were transferred from Celebici to Musala, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 9th December 1992 I was transferred to Musala, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In some time around January 1993, in the MUP of Konjic, you again made a statement, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave so many statements at all sorts of places that I really cannot recall them all or the places where I gave them. I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There in MUP, as you were making the statement, you were not maltreated by anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not. Not in the MUP. I was not maltreated while making that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you signed that statement as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, I had to sign the statement lest I be again treated with the same treatment, beating and so on, as I have already described. I was afraid; my life was threatened in my view.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask that the witness be shown this statement of January 15th 1993 to see whether it is indeed his signature. At the same time, I shall have a copy submitted also to the Prosecutor and the judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I raise a matter at this time? Your Honours, the statement that I anticipate is going to be shown to the witness is a statement that was taken by the people, the very people that were holding him captive. He has already said in his evidence that he had to sign anything that was put in front of him, so terrified was he of the circumstances in which he found himself. Your Honours, under Rule 95 of the Rules of the Tribunal, it is provided for that no evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability, or if its admission is anti-ethical or would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. In my submission, your Honour, this very document falls exactly into that category, and, in my submission, for the Tribunal to entertain any cross-examination in relation to this document, it would have to be done in such a way, in my submission, as to be consistent with Rule 91, to be so categorised as a document that was obtained in circumstances where the witness could not freely and voluntarily provide the information that is contained therein. He has also mentioned the fact that at that stage, he signed practically anything -- he said he would have to sign anything that was put in front of him at that stage. Your Honours, I am not objecting to a form of cross-examination, provided there is no suggestion at any stage that what is contained in the statement is in any way true or correct. If it is not asserted by the cross-examination that the contents of the statement are true and correct, then I do not have any objection to it, but if it is sought to challenge the credibility of this witness through this document, then, having regard to the circumstances under which it was obtained, I say it offends Rule 95 and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms Residovic, have you any reply to that objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. It was in a similar way that we conducted discussion before this Trial Chamber, but I believe that now the court has in front of it proof, evidence which are contrary to what my distinguished colleague has just stated, namely we have interviewed a member of the Commission as a witness of the prosecution, and the prosecution side gave those persons very high grade in terms of their professional attitude and correct attitude in the way they were taking those statements. On the other hand, this witness, in answering the prosecution's questions, clearly said that while he was being held in the Musala prison, he made a statement -- first of all that he had not been maltreated there at all; secondly that this statement in MUP, Konjic -- when answering my question, he said that he did make it, that everybody treated him correctly, that he had signed that statement. What the significance of the content of that statement will be is something for the court to assess, but these are all circumstances which warrant the defence's presentation of this particular statement given in Konjic to the witness to recognise his signature, and that this statement should actually be used for the purposes of defence, which is to say in connection with the credibility of this witness. I have established the basis for this particular use of this statement, because we presented to the witness these statements that he gave in Belgrade, that he gave to the investigator of this Tribunal. I believe all this will be quite sufficient for this Tribunal to assess the credibility of this witness. Therefore I move that these statements be given to the witness so that he could recognise his signature and that they be used for the purposes as evidence of the defence for the purposes proposed by the defence in this procedure. Normally, the defence will, in the stage of presenting its own evidence, bring in other evidence to corroborate these circumstances. It will be up to the Tribunal to assign various degrees of credibility to each such piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, my understanding of the approach you have adopted is that you are impeaching the credit of the witness by using two statements which he has earlier made, the statement to the prosecution and the statement which he made when he was in detention. These are the things you are using in impeaching his credit. What Mr. Niemann is objecting to is the validity of using the statement made by a witness under incarceration as inconsistent with Rule 95. I agree you have argued that the prosecution has called as its witness one of the members of the committee which had taken such statements, but, notwithstanding that, whether such statements are within the general penumbra of Rule 95 is what Mr. Niemann is arguing about. But you did appear to have responded to that aspect of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, is it a rule that any statement made by a detainee is treated to be as one obtained under caution? Is it a rule that every statement has to be taken in the light of the background in which it is made?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honours. Clearly a statement can be taken from a witness in detention. The issue of voluntariness becomes very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is my question. Supposing the defence leaks evidence at some stage showing they were voluntarily made then, it will have a handicap that this statement was never shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would suggest that from what the witness has already said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let us mark it for identification purposes. If the defence can lead evidence to show it was obtained voluntarily, then of course we can look at it; otherwise we will just exclude it from evidence. At this stage, maybe show it for the purpose of identification. Does it bear your signature? That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear him reply completely to the circumstances in which the statement was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours have heard extensive evidence about the conditions -- does your Honour want me to address this issue or just put the statement to the witness? I am sorry, I misunderstood what your Honour was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is no rule that any statement made under detention has to be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not suggesting that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: At this stage, show it for purposes of identification; does it bear your signature or not? It is for the defence to show whether this statement was made voluntarily. At this stage if the defence is denied that opportunity, later on if it has found some statements were made voluntarily, then your objection will be: the witness was never shown this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no objection to that, your Honours. There was only one other matter I wanted to correct. It is not strictly speaking correct to say that the witness was not mistreated in the Musala camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The statements probably would be viewed with some suspicion, but the defence can remove that suspicion if it is possible for them to lead evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So long as they attempt to do that and are successful in doing that, then I will have no objection. Certainly I submit that they should go at least through the process of establishing voluntariness before they do so. I might just add, your Honours, that mere signature, of course, as your Honours know, is not sufficient to establish voluntariness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask the witness to identify his signature, that this statement be taken for purposes of identification, I do not wish to repeat that the Prosecutor asks every witness whether any proceedings had been instituted against him when such proof is offered and we have objections of this kind, so I should like to ask now that the witness recognise his signature and the defence will tender this as evidence after having also manifested other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just have to say something. I gave the statement in MUP Konjic several times. I do not know whether you are referring to that statement. Two days before giving that statement, I was subjected to a mock execution. I can describe how it was: we went to the hill at Prenj to dig trenches, and the soldiers up there on those positions -- I believe their names are there, the name of their Muslim formation was the Muderizi -- they were there on this hill at Prenj and as I was digging the trench, please let me describe this, this soldier came up to me and he asked me as I was digging what my name was. I normally stood to attention, I had to. I told him what my name was, then three or four more of them came. Everything I am saying can be confirmed by Tomic Bozo, by Dordic Zdravko, also camp inmates, the latter one being from the village of Bradina. Let me please finish --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is not my question. If your Honours wish to hear this witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please let me finish before you show me the statement. One of those soldiers told me to face him, turn around and face him. He raised his rifle, he repeated, I think it was a PAP, it was an automatic rifle, I am not sure. Normally I was extremely scared. He shot from the rifle, of course I was terrified. They started laughing. One of the soldiers said: "That was a manoeuvring bullet in the rifle." I, of course, was not aware of that, I thought my end had come, and I was subjected to this mock execution several times. I did not know that it would be a mock execution. This particular incident took place two days prior to my making the statement in the SUP of Konjic. I gave many statements in the SUP of Konjic, I do not know whether you are referring to that particular one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to show you this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was afraid I would be subjected to the same kind of treatment as the one I was given in Celebici which I really took very hard because I would be beaten three times per day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has now been going on for three or four minutes without one question being asked. He has just decided to start making statements to the court. Part of that is because we have -- when there is a legal objection and the lawyers talk about that legal objection, we do it in a way that the witness can hear what we are saying and then the witness feels like he somehow has to engage himself in the legal issues that we are talking about. That is what he is doing now. He has decided to launch off in giving information that nobody asked him about; nobody asked him a question that caused him to give us all this information just now. If he has been asked a proper question, fine, let him answer it properly, but the court must control the situation of witnesses just popping off without a question being asked. That is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think counsel has a better advantage to assisting the court than the witness. No counsel has that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you taken a look; did you see your signature? Is that your signature, Mr. Vukalo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems so. It seems that this is what I sign.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this a signature identical to the one which you affixed to the statement that you made to the investigators of the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am only asking: is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they had told me that it was night and it was day I would have had to say it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am not talking about the content, I am talking about the signature. You have recognised your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to stress the circumstances under which I signed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the witness has identified his signature, and at this moment I move that this particular statement only be accepted as a statement which has been identified, and at this moment I propose it as defence exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just that it is signed, because he disowns the contents altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Vukalo. Just a couple of brief questions. You know Ivica Buric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You saw Ivica Buric in Celebici, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivica Buric is one of the first Croats in the village of Pokojiste to put on a camouflage uniform. I saw him in Pokojiste when I was in Branko Jozic's house when I was actually taken to that house and had to lie against the wall.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also saw him in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that I saw him in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Ivica Buric, on one occasion, filmed you in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one in Celebici, in camp. I thought you were referring to Ivica Buric from the village of Pokojiste. No, that is Ivica Kozora. I got mixed up. I know Ivica Buric from the camp, yes, when I was in number 6. I do, I remember him well. I will never forget when he brought this camera. When I was beaten like I have never been beaten in my life before and he filmed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then you were given to read something, were you not, and you would not and then Ivica Buric and Dedic beat you up so viciously that you will never forget it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not Ivica Buric that beat me up, it was Zenga and Osmo Dedic that beat me up. Ivica Buric was filming this. I was totally naked and they hit me with a soldier's belt; Zenga and Dedic Osmo did. I was all black and blue from my heels up to the top of my head. That is the way I went back -- that is the state in which I went back to number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Vukalo. I have no further questions for you. Thank you. Thank you, your Honours. I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before you start, let me give this caution. Mr. Ackerman has just finished his comment on the supervision of the Trial Chamber by asking the Trial Chamber to tell a witness to stop saying certain things. As far as this Trial Chamber is concerned, when a witness is making a statement and saying things which are relevant to questions asked to him, or are related to them, I think this witness's statement is entitled to as much respect as to what counsel might be able to offer. I do not think it is the place of counsel to tell the Trial Chamber what to accept, except in a more formal situation where objection is raised as to that part of the statement. I do not think counsel is entitled to a better advantage, as I said before, in assisting the Trial Chamber than as any other witness who is entitled to assist the Trial Chamber in getting to the justice of the matter we have before us. So you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just say, I think perhaps I was misunderstood. My complaint and my objection was this: that when counsel are engaged in arguing a legal point, I think it is inappropriate for the witness to participate in that argument by offering his own opinions by factual information or otherwise as to how the outcome of that legal issue should be involved. As far as what this Chamber does with regard to the witness answering questions, that is absolutely this Chamber's prerogative. I am just objecting that witnesses should not be permitted to engage in the legal arguments that are going on between counsel and should remain silent until that is completed and another question is put to him. That was the force of what I was trying to suggest. I apparently did it inartfully and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have told you exactly what the position should be. I do not think anyone in this Trial Chamber understood what the witness was saying as relevant to what was going on. Now Mr. Olujic, you may proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Vukalo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Before we start with my cross-examination, will you please bear in mind the warnings given yesterday regarding the technical aspect of the proceedings and that is that you should wait for my question to be interpreted, and only when you hear the English interpretation you should answer, so that everyone can follow our conversation without us engaging in a dialogue. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vukalo, in the course of your direct examination, you said that you knew Mr. Pavo Mucic or Zdravko Mucic, and that he would be away up to as many as ten days from the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did Mr. Mucic beat you ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mucic ever present when you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw him, but I said that as the commander of the camp he should have known what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Please, I have noticed that in your wish to assist the court -- you are a witness here and I understand you. I also have understanding because of the terrible experiences you have gone through, but I appeal to you in the interest of efficiency that when I ask you questions, will you please answer them, only those questions that I put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: If you act that way, you will make it easier for both of us to get through this quickly. Thank you, Mr. Vukalo. Mr. Vukalo, you said that Mr. Mucic wore a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he would come in uniform as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you see any sign of rank on those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there were none?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot claim that there were any, nor that there were none; I just do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mucic an officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he held the position of camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether he was an officer; you know what an officer is. When you went to the JNA, you know what officers are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you say that he wore a uniform, the uniform of which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A camouflage uniform, I do not remember any insignia. He never had a cap on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was it the kind of uniform that more or less all persons were wearing who were involved in one way or another in the operations on all three sides, simply a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing the same kind of uniform as the guards in Celebici, or some of the guards, the same kind as the guards, camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know Davor Bendzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was Davor Bendzo a friend of Mr. Mucic's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was; at least while I was in the camp he would talk to him outside and inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell me: you spent quite a long time in the camp, until December 1992, I mean Celebici camp. During that time, while you were detained in the camp, was there any raising of the flag every morning in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was in number 6, I could not see that anyway, so I do not know. I do not know at all. I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear the anthem being played?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about that either, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see any formal lining up of troops within the grounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when the oath was taken by the Muslim army. I remember when Zenga and Dedic Osmo took my clothes off and beat me with belts and Ivica Buric, whom I have just mentioned, was filming me and on the wall to the right where I was being beaten, there were I do not know how many troops who were there to take their oath of allegiance and they were applauding and laughing. I know that this taking of the oath did take place within the camp grounds because we could hear it. We could hear it in hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was this in the part where the troops were or where you were as prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time, I was in hangar number 6 and we heard and later learnt that they were -- that the Muslim army was taking an oath of allegiance and we could hear the music too, but I did not see it actually taking place. It must have been nearby somewhere, near the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, of course, from your direct knowledge whether you ever witnessed any quarrels among the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards having disputes among themselves? I did not see or hear it myself, but I heard from other guards, as if apparently Zenga and Delic had a fight over something, but I did not hear much about it. I heard this from other guards and from other detainees. There were some stories to that effect, that they had had a quarrel, why and how I do not know, and that after that, Zenga was absent from the camp for a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to these answers. He says he does not know, he found out from people in the camp, that he has no personal knowledge about this occurrence, and he keeps going on. I object to no personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you have any other questions to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Tell me, Mr. Vukalo, the different kinds of uniforms that you saw in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the camouflage uniform was most widespread.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were there uniforms of the TO, territorial defence, the MUP, the military police, the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do I know? I was most worried over myself and I was terrified and thinking only how I could avoid beatings, so I did not really take much notice of the uniforms, but I did see the camouflage uniforms. I even saw the signs of the moon and stars on a cap called the fez.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So there were all kinds of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say there were all kinds. Camouflage uniforms were most widespread. There may have been others, but I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the communist party, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, up to 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not until 1990. I was a member in 1986 or 1985, but by 1987 I stopped being a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: From your personal data, we see that you are now living in Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not living in Samac, I do not have a place to live really nor do I have any permanent employment. My house was burnt down, I have no property whatever; wherever I can find a job I live, and that is how I am making ends meet. Sometimes in Serbia, somewhere or anywhere I can find a job, that is where I live, so I do not have any permanent residence or any house or flat or anything. Until something changes, I suppose one day it will. I had everything; unfortunately it was burned down. I have been destroyed financially, in every respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Have the authorities in the place where you are living assisted you in finding a job? Have they given you any material relief, any assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you talk with the refugees and misplaced persons and others from Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are no refugees from Celebici. Let me repeat again that I do not live in one particular place on a permanent basis; I just look where I can find a job and I stay there for a while and then move on with my wife and child.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In the course of your direct examination, you said that there were massive beatings, as you described them, mass beatings, and that on one occasion, all the prisoners in hangar number 6 were beaten; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several of these mass beatings, I cannot say exactly how often they occurred, they were not too often, but they did occur several times and I remember that we were all beaten when the International Red Cross had registered us and left; then we were all given a hiding. If necessary, I can describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at 12.00. (11.30 am) (A short break) (12.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, you are still cross-examining, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Thank you. Mr. Vukalo, let us continue this cross-examination. We will be through soon, so I would like to remind you, as I did at the beginning, to be as concise as possible and to answer the questions put to you, as you did, more or less, in the first part of my cross-examination. Mr. Vukalo, in the course of your examination-in-chief, you mentioned Donje Selo, which is close to your village, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which testimony, here?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Donje Selo is about three kilometres from the beginning of my village and I was at the far end of this village in the hamlet of Vukalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What did you say about Donje Selo, could you tell me please? You mentioned Donje Selo; that is why I am asking you and now you have repeated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know where Donje Selo is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You also said that it is about 3 kilometres from your village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cerici and Donje Selo are one next to the other and from there to the beginning of my village is about 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned in the course of the direct examination, and when I say that I am referring to what you had said yesterday in court -- you said, with reference to Donje Selo, that they were organised for defence, but not very well; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall -- actually I do not know whether they were organised at all. I just do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the villagers of Donje Selo had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was in the Celebici camp, there were detainees from Donje Selo, though I do not know much about it, but I heard that there was some weapons that were surrendered and I heard this from the detainees, but I do not know much myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard in Celebici camp that they had a few, I do not know how many, a few automatic rifles, M48. How many, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was any kind of village guard duty organised there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps they did have guard duty, but I do not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me please whether you know somebody known as Focak? He was a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you have just reminded me. He was known as Focak and he worked in the prison in Foca. He was some kind of investigator there, I think. Whether he was or not, I do not know. He too was one of the ones who interrogated us. He was a guard, but he also did the interrogations for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What did he interrogate you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, but I cannot remember too well, how I was apprehended and brought to the camp, to the building and then they asked whether I knew -- whether anybody was armed in Bjelovcina, whether anybody was in hiding there. That is as much as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And what was your answer to Focak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what I said, but I think that I said that I did not know whether there were any people there in Bjelovcina. I said that most of us men had been arrested and detained in Konjic at the camp there and in Celebici, that most of the people from the village of Bjelovcina. All the younger men were incarcerated in Celebici and in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: During the interrogation by Focak, was any coercion used against you? Were you physically mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I was interrogated, many other detainees were interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I am asking about you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But let me say this. Many others were interrogated like Vukasin Mr.kajic. He was beaten and hit both when he was taken there and during the questioning, according to what Vukasin Mr.kajic told us when he came back, so he was beaten also on the way back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Witness, the question is directed to you. It is not about other detainees. Counsel is asking whether you were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was taken to Focak, I was slapped and hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did Focak mistreat you during the interrogation; that is all I am asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be kind enough, you said during your testimony that your village had been shelled; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As together with the other people from my hamlet and with the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether your village was shelled, as you said during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard two shells somewhere at the beginning of the village of Bjelovcina, in the direction of Donje Selo, but I cannot say anything with certainty about that, but I know that Jovo Gotovac was killed and Uros Djurica or were killed by those shells. I learnt about that at the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The detainees from the village of Bjelovcina who were brought in later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can you give me the name and surname of those people who told you that these people were killed by the shells that fell on your village, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. I was told by Dusan Tomic, Ranko Tomic and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me, please: in your village did you have a village leader, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean a military leader or commander? No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But how is that possible? A war was in the making, you have no weapons, and you do not even have anybody who might be in charge of the organisation. Maybe you do not know the name of that person, or you are excluding the possibility that there was a leader of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware at all that there were any leaders. We did not have educated people in the village actually, and I really do not see who could have assumed such a role.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So your answer is that there were no such people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukalo. I pass the witness. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could again have a little bit of time to get wired up? May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: My name is Tom Moran, I am an attorney and I represent a man named Hazim Delic. I am going to ask you some questions. If at any time you do not understand one of the questions I ask, will you please stop me and ask me to repeat it or rephrase it, because frankly I do not sometimes phrase questions as well as I probably should. Will you do that for me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, would you please also listen to my questions and answer the question that I ask you? If you do, this will go a whole lot quicker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. One other thing, you have been very, very good about this so far during both your direct and your cross-examinations, but sometimes witnesses get into conversation, people want to nod their heads, yes or no. If you look round the courtroom you see two ladies with strange looking machines; they are called court reporters. They have to write down everything we say. They cannot write down a nod. If you say yes or no when that is appropriate, could you do that also, sir. Then also sir, if at any time you want to stop and think for a second, if you feel like you are confused or something like that, let me know and we will work it out. Okay sir? Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir, the first thing I would like to ask you about is this: do you recall an incident some time when you were in the camp, Celebici, probably in July, when some Arab journalists came to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, tell the judges what occurred while those Arab journalists were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When those Arab journalists came, we were glad, hoping and thinking that somebody had come to change our plight, to alleviate our suffering. However when they visited hangar number 6, we were beaten and hit. I was one of those who were beaten, I remember that, and Milovan Kuljanin had to go on his knees and pray, some kind of prayer, the Muslim prayer. I know that we were hit and beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, did the Arab journalists film this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were filming something, but I do not know whether they filmed this in particular, so I was mainly concerned with myself. I did see them filming something, I do not know whether they filmed that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, some of these members of the TV crew actually took part in the beatings, did they not? They beat you, for instance, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not the members of the team, the members of the crew; they did not beat me, but the guards did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: They made some of the detainees make confessions in front of the cameras, like Rajko Djordjic, did they not? Did not the guards and the TV crew make him admit in front of the cameras that they committed all kinds of crimes against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember what you said about Rajko Djordjic. I was just saying, sir, that I was worried for my own safety, so I did not dare look much. We all realised, actually, that these were not the people that we had thought that we could be frank with, and tell them in Cerici what was troubling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, the bottom line is this TV crew, these journalists, were basically bad people, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, since they watched us being beaten and some of them were even laughing. They were not good people from my point of view and from the point of view of the other detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, let me talk about another event which I do not think you have talked about on either your direct or any of the cross. Do you remember back some time in August my client Mr. Delic came into hangar 6 with a list of names of people to be released; do you remember that occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please explain it a little? To be released home, or what, if anybody had a home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What I am saying is: some time in August 1992, after the Red Cross visit, Mr. Delic came into hangar 6 and read out a list of names of people who were to be released from custody to go about their business, were not to be transferred to another camp but actually to be sent home if they had homes, or just released. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Celebici was not a detention centre, it was a camp. At least that is what I think. There were many occasions when some detainees went to Konjic, to the sports hall at Musala, or a fewer number were released, to Donje Selo, where many of them -- where many of the inhabitants of Bjelovcina were put up in Donje Selo, in some kind of a house arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is what I am talking about, the first time that occurred, sir. Do you remember Mr. Delic calling out Branko Sudar's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. Perhaps, I just cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. If you do not remember, that is fine, sir. That is no problem at all. Sir, let me ask you this: who have you talked with and discussed with what you are going to testify about today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean? Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: For instance, since you came to The Hague, outside of the courtroom, have you discussed your testimony with anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spoke with Mr. Grant, the Prosecutor. I do not think I spoke to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How long was the conversation with Mr. Grant? By the way, just for the record, that would be Mr. Niemann, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I spoke with Mr. Grant; I cannot tell you exactly how long it took.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Was it a long time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice, I think, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Was it a long time or a short time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last conversation we had was a very brief one. It was not long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That was the one yesterday when he asked you if you would agree not to have a television interview; is that the one you are talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was that, and also I was in a room here for maybe 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Those were the two times you discussed your testimony with Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I spoke before that -- I think it was Tuesday or Wednesday -- no Wednesday. I spoke to him I think three times, but yesterday it was very brief, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about the other conversations? Were they long conversations, sir, or were they short conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
